screens.title: Introduction to AWS Direct Connect (DX)
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we'll build an intuitive, practical understanding of AWS Direct Connect. Direct Connect is a physical, private network link into AWS that bypasses the public internet. That private path gives you consistent throughput, lower and more predictable latency, and often lower costs for moving large volumes of data. As you learn, think of Direct Connect as a private highway built between your data center and AWS. Unlike an encrypted tunnel over the internet, this highway keeps traffic off public routing, which reduces congestion, jitter, and packet loss for mission-critical services. We'll also cover when Direct Connect matters: hybrid applications that need LAN-like behavior, large data migrations and analytics transfers, low-latency use cases such as voice or trading systems, and situations where compliance forbids public internet transit. Finally, you'll see the basic elements that make a DX link work — the physical cross-connect at a Direct Connect location, Border Gateway Protocol peering, and logical virtual interfaces to reach VPCs or public AWS services. By the end, you'll be able to decide when Direct Connect is the right architectural choice and what components you must plan for. Consider: which of your current workloads would need the steadiness of a private highway versus the flexibility of a VPN?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: In this section we'll set clear objectives so you know the skills you'll build. First, you'll be able to explain the core purpose and benefits of AWS Direct Connect: how a dedicated, private physical link changes performance, predictability, and cost profiles compared with internet-based VPN. You will learn to describe that Direct Connect bypasses the public internet, reducing congestion and making throughput and latency far more consistent for production services. Second, you will identify scenarios where Direct Connect matters most. These include hybrid cloud architectures that require near-LAN performance between on-premises systems and VPCs, large data migrations to S3 or analytics stores, and low-latency applications such as VoIP or trading platforms. You will also recognize compliance-driven use cases where data must not traverse public internet paths. Each objective ties theory to concrete operational decisions, so you'll practice mapping workloads to connectivity choices. Finally, we’ll introduce the verification milestone you can use to confirm competency: a short design exercise recommending Direct Connect or VPN for a specified workload. Keep thinking about a workload you manage and whether it needs the private highway Direct Connect provides.

screens.title: What is AWS Direct Connect?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Direct Connect is a service that provides a physical, private network connection between a customer's network and AWS. In plain language, picture a private highway between your data center and AWS that traffic uses instead of the public road network. This dedicates fiber capacity to your traffic and avoids the routing unpredictability of the public internet. The key claim to remember is this: Direct Connect gives you private, consistent connectivity — not automatic encryption. From an operational standpoint, that means you order a cross-connect at a Direct Connect location, install or request a port, then configure your edge router to peer with AWS using BGP. A common concrete example is database replication between on-premises systems and an Amazon VPC. With Direct Connect, the replication stream experiences fewer interruptions and steady throughput, so replication completes in predictable windows. A typical misconception is to assume Direct Connect encrypts traffic by default; it does not provide end-to-end encryption. If confidentiality is required, you should layer an IPsec VPN over the Direct Connect link. That combination gives you the privacy and low latency of a dedicated path with the encryption guarantees of a VPN. As you plan, ask: do I require encryption in transit? If yes, prepare to configure a VPN overlay or application-level encryption.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is AWS Direct Connect?
Direct Connect — plain definition
A private physical connection into AWS that bypasses the public internet to deliver predictable bandwidth and latency.
Analogy

Think of it as your own dedicated highway into AWS, where traffic doesn't mix with general internet cars. That reduces jams and unpredictable slowdowns.

Operational example

Use Direct Connect for continuous database replication from your data center to a VPC to ensure predictable replication windows.

Common misconception

Direct Connect does not encrypt traffic by default. If encryption is required, layer an IPsec VPN over the link or use application-level encryption.

Key Takeaway

Direct Connect provides private, reliable bandwidth to AWS but requires you to add encryption if confidentiality is needed.

Components in focus
  • Direct Connect location: physical facility where AWS equipment is located.
  • Cross-connect: fiber between your device and the AWS router.
  • Virtual Interface (VIF): logical interface used to reach VPCs or AWS public services.
  • BGP: used to exchange routes between your router and AWS.
Tip: Record the cross-connect ID and VLAN when ordering a port — these are required by most colocation providers.

screens.title: Direct Connect vs. Site-to-Site VPN
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN helps you choose the right link for a workload. Site-to-Site VPN runs encrypted tunnels over the public internet. It is quick to deploy and can be a good short-term or backup option, but its performance depends on internet routing and can vary due to congestion and routing changes. Direct Connect, in contrast, establishes a private physical path that bypasses internet routing, delivering steady throughput and reduced latency. That steadiness matters for migrations, replication, and real-time applications. In cost terms, Direct Connect often reduces per-gigabyte transfer costs for high-volume traffic, but it does require port or circuit ordering and possibly colocation fees. A common operational pattern is to use Direct Connect as the primary link and keep VPN as a failover for resilience. Another misconception to avoid is assuming VPN always provides equal security to Direct Connect: VPN provides encryption over the internet, while Direct Connect provides a private path but not automatic encryption. For workloads requiring both privacy and encryption, the recommended approach is to run an IPsec VPN tunnel over the Direct Connect link. That design gives predictable performance and the encryption properties you need. When making a decision, weigh deployment time, monthly port costs, predictable SLAs, and the sensitivity of your data.

keyIdea.title: Choice factors
keyIdea.text: VPN is fast to deploy and encrypted over the internet; Direct Connect gives predictable, private paths and often lower per-GB costs for sustained high-volume traffic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › DX vs VPN
Comparison table
Performance & Predictability
Direct Connect provides steady throughput and lower jitter. VPN performance depends on public internet routing and is variable.
Winner: Direct Connect
Security & Encryption
VPN provides encryption over the internet. Direct Connect provides a private path but not end-to-end encryption without an overlay.
Different strengths
Cost & Scale
Direct Connect can lower per-GB costs for sustained high-volume traffic but requires provisioning. VPN has minimal setup cost but higher per-GB internet transfer costs.
Depends on volume
Design tip: Use Direct Connect for primary traffic and VPN as a failover to combine predictable throughput and redundancy.
Concrete scenario
Your analytics cluster ingests 10 TB per day from on-prem storage. If you use VPN, daily throughput may vary and nightly jobs might overrun. Using Direct Connect helps keep ingestion within known windows.
Common mistake

Assuming Direct Connect is encrypted by default. Always plan encryption overlays if required by policy.

Key Takeaway

Match Direct Connect when you need predictability and sustained bandwidth; use VPN for quick, encrypted internet tunnels or as backup.

screens.title: Hybrid Cloud with Direct Connect
screens.narratorSegment: Hybrid cloud architectures combine on-premises resources with cloud-based services. Direct Connect helps these environments behave like a unified network by offering consistent, low-jitter connectivity between your data center and AWS. This matters when applications require frequent synchronous calls, for example between a local identity service and a cloud-hosted application, or when you run distributed databases that replicate between sites. With a Direct Connect link and BGP peering, your on-prem routes and VPC routes can be exchanged so that application traffic follows a predictable path. An operational example: you have an on-prem authentication server that must validate millions of logins per day for a cloud application. With Direct Connect the auth traffic experiences fewer spikes and session timeouts than over the public internet, improving user experience. A misconception is to treat Direct Connect as a drop-in replacement for a LAN; it provides LAN-like predictability for routed traffic but still requires careful design for failover, routing preferences, and security zones. Always plan for redundancy by pairing Direct Connect with a backup VPN or a second DX connection in another location. Consider the routing policies you will configure in BGP to prefer the private path and define fallback behavior for outages.

keyIdea.text: Direct Connect reduces variability between on-prem and cloud networks, enabling near-LAN performance for hybrid applications while still requiring routing and redundancy planning.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Hybrid Cloud
Architecture pattern
Use Direct Connect to create a private routed path between on-premises and VPCs. Exchange routes via BGP and use VIFs to direct traffic to specific services.
Why it matters
Predictable connections reduce application errors and make replication and synchronization windows reliable.
Example
On-prem identity servers handle validation for cloud apps. Direct Connect reduces login time variability and session dropped rates compared to internet paths.
Common mistake
Assuming a single Direct Connect link is sufficient for resilience. Always design redundancy and failover strategies.
Practical considerations
  • BGP policies: define route preference to prefer DX routes and fall back to VPN or internet when necessary.
  • VLANs & VIFs: separate traffic types (private VPC access vs public service access) with appropriate VIFs.
  • Redundancy: include a backup connection or VPN for failover and maintenance windows.
Key Takeaway

Direct Connect makes hybrid systems more predictable, but you must design BGP, VIFs, and redundancy deliberately.

screens.title: Large Data Transfers and Migration
screens.narratorSegment: Large-scale data transfers are one of the clearest use cases for Direct Connect. Moving many terabytes or petabytes over the public internet can be slow, unpredictable, and expensive. Direct Connect delivers higher sustained throughput and can reduce transfer times from weeks to days. To make an informed decision, you should estimate transfer time using a simple formula: convert total data to bits, divide by your effective bandwidth in bits per second, and then convert to hours or days. For example, for 50 terabytes, multiply by eight to get bits, then divide by effective throughput. Remember to account for utilization — your link will rarely be 100 percent used. A typical planning step is to assume 70–80 percent utilization to capture realistic throughput. Another practical consideration is cost: Direct Connect often lowers per-gigabyte charges for sustained outbound traffic, but you must evaluate port costs and any colocation fees. A common error is to assume line rate equals effective throughput. Always apply utilization and overhead for protocol and storage performance when estimating. Finally, consider parallelization or staging transfers: using multiple connections or dedicated appliances for bulk import can shorten windows and distribute load safely.

keyIdea.title: Transfer planning
keyIdea.text: Estimate transfer time using total bits divided by effective throughput and account for utilization and overhead; Direct Connect reduces transfer time for sustained large transfers.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Large Data Transfer
Estimate transfer time
Formula to plan: Time = Total data in bits ÷ Effective bandwidth (bps). Remember to include utilization.
Calculation example (concept)
# Example variables
# 50 TB total data
# Convert to bits and divide by effective bandwidth
Remember: utilization and protocol overhead reduce the effective throughput. Plan using realistic utilization values such as 0.7 or 0.8 rather than 1.0.
Key Takeaway

Use the bits-over-bandwidth formula and realistic utilization to estimate migration windows; Direct Connect shortens those windows for high-volume transfers.

Practical steps
  1. Calculate total data in bits (bytes × 8).
  2. Choose bandwidth and realistic utilization.
  3. Divide bits by effective bps to get seconds; convert to hours/days.
  4. Compare results for VPN vs Direct Connect and include costs.
Scenario
For a sustained migration, Direct Connect often makes multi-day transfers possible and predictable instead of indefinite and variable over VPN.

screens.title: Estimating Transfer Time — Worked Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a specific calculation so you can apply the formula confidently. Start with 50 terabytes of data. Convert bytes to bits by multiplying by eight. Using the common convention from this chapter, 1 TB is approximated as ten to the twelfth bytes. So 50 TB becomes 50 times ten to the twelfth bytes, multiplied by eight to convert to bits. Next pick bandwidth and utilization. For a 100 megabit connection with 80 percent utilization, the effective bandwidth is 100 megabits per second times 0.8, which results in 80 megabits per second. Divide the total bits by the effective bandwidth in bits per second to get the total seconds, then convert to hours and days. For the 100 megabit example, the result is about 58 days. For a 1 gigabit connection at the same utilization, the math yields about 5.8 days. These numbers show the order-of-magnitude impact of bandwidth: a tenfold increase in line-rate cuts the migration window by roughly ten. A common misuse is to forget utilization; assuming full line-rate will produce optimistic and risky schedules. Use these calculations to set realistic migration targets and to compare VPN and Direct Connect options.

keyIdea.title: Worked math
keyIdea.text: 50 TB at 80% utilization: ~58 days on 100 Mbps vs ~5.8 days on 1 Gbps, demonstrating the large impact of bandwidth on migration windows.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Transfer Calculation
Calculation steps
  1. Total bits = 50 TB × 10^12 bytes/TB × 8 bits/byte = 400 × 10^12 bits.
  2. Effective bandwidth = advertised bandwidth × utilization.
  3. Time (seconds) = total bits ÷ effective bandwidth (bps).
  4. Convert seconds → hours → days.
# Conceptual python-style snippet (illustration, not executed)
data_tb = 50
data_bits = data_tb * 8 * (10**12)  # 1 TB = 10^12 bytes
vpn_bandwidth_bps = 100 * (10**6)   # 100 Mbps
dx_bandwidth_bps = 1000 * (10**6)   # 1 Gbps
utilization = 0.8
effective_vpn = vpn_bandwidth_bps * utilization
effective_dx = dx_bandwidth_bps * utilization
# compute seconds and convert to days
Results (rounded)
100 Mbps @ 80%: Effective 80 Mbps → ~5,000,000 seconds → ~1,388.9 hours → ~57.9 days.
1 Gbps @ 80%: Effective 800 Mbps → ~500,000 seconds → ~138.9 hours → ~5.8 days.
Interpretation
A single order-of-magnitude increase in bandwidth reduces migration time by roughly the same factor. This is why Direct Connect ports or multiple circuits can be decisive for large migrations.
Key Takeaway

Always factor utilization into bandwith-based migration estimates and use Direct Connect for predictable bulk transfers.

screens.title: Low-latency Apps and Compliance Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Certain applications require low latency and consistent packet delivery, such as voice conferencing, real-time streaming, and financial trading systems. These workloads are sensitive to jitter and packet loss, and they benefit from the predictable path that Direct Connect provides. A private physical link reduces variability and gives you a stable baseline for latency-sensitive design. In addition, organizations operating under strict compliance or regulatory frameworks may prohibit transmitting sensitive data over the public internet. Direct Connect provides a private conduit into AWS that helps meet such policies because traffic does not traverse public internet routing. However, remember that Direct Connect does not, by itself, provide end-to-end encryption required by some compliance regimes. When encryption is mandated, you should layer an IPsec VPN over the Direct Connect link to provide both a private path and encryption. A common misconception is to conflate privacy with encryption: private connectivity reduces exposure to internet-based attackers but does not replace cryptographic protection. When you design for regulated environments, combine Direct Connect for path control with an encryption overlay and prove your configuration in an audit scenario. Also plan for logging and access controls at endpoints to satisfy compliance evidence requirements.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Low-Latency & Compliance
Latency-sensitive design
Direct Connect reduces jitter and provides a predictable baseline for designs that need consistent packet delivery and low latency.
Example
VoIP and streaming platforms see fewer dropped calls and smoother playback when using a private link compared with internet paths.
Compliance note
Direct Connect helps meet policies that forbid public internet transit, but encryption overlays may still be required for end-to-end confidentiality.
Design checklist
  • Confirm regulatory requirements for encryption and data residency.
  • Plan an IPsec overlay if cryptographic protection is required.
  • Design BGP failover and a backup VPN for continuity.
  • Ensure logging and audit evidence at endpoints.
Key Takeaway

Direct Connect is well suited for jitter-sensitive and compliance-sensitive workloads, but combine path control with encryption where policies require it.

screens.title: Core Components of a Direct Connect Link
screens.narratorSegment: Establishing a Direct Connect link requires coordinating several technical components. First, at your site you need a router capable of BGP peering; BGP is the routing protocol used to exchange prefixes with AWS. Second, a Direct Connect location is the physical facility that houses AWS networking equipment; you or your colocation provider must provision a cross-connect between your device and the AWS router in that location. Third, once the physical layer is active, you create virtual interfaces — VIFs — which are logical connections over the physical link. VIFs can be private (to reach VPCs), public (to reach AWS public services), or hosted. Fourth, you will configure BGP sessions across the VIF to advertise and receive routes. An important operational detail is documenting the cross-connect ID, VLAN, and your autonomous system number (ASN) ahead of provisioning. Another practical note: Direct Connect does not automatically provide encryption nor automatic redundancy, so you may want to order multiple ports or plan a VPN overlay for failover. A common misconception is to assume the cloud side will configure your router; in reality you must coordinate both sides of the peering and validate route advertisements and route preferences. Preparing a checklist for the colo provider and your networking team avoids delays during provisioning.

narration.text: Establishing a Direct Connect link requires coordinating several technical components. First, at your site you need a router capable of BGP peering; BGP is the routing protocol used to exchange prefixes with AWS. Second, a Direct Connect location is the physical facility that houses AWS networking equipment; you or your colocation provider must provision a cross-connect between your device and the AWS router in that location. Third, once the physical layer is active, you create virtual interfaces — VIFs — which are logical connections over the physical link. VIFs can be private (to reach VPCs), public (to reach AWS public services), or hosted. Fourth, you will configure BGP sessions across the VIF to advertise and receive routes. An important operational detail is documenting the cross-connect ID, VLAN, and your autonomous system number (ASN) ahead of provisioning. Another practical note: Direct Connect does not automatically provide encryption nor automatic redundancy, so you may want to order multiple ports or plan a VPN overlay for failover. A common misconception is to assume the cloud side will configure your router; in reality you must coordinate both sides of the peering and validate route advertisements and route preferences. Preparing a checklist for the colo provider and your networking team avoids delays during provisioning.

screens.title: Encryption, Privacy, and Overlays
screens.narratorSegment: Security planning for Direct Connect requires clear separation between path privacy and cryptographic encryption. Direct Connect provides a private physical path that keeps traffic off the public internet, which reduces exposure and can help satisfy policy constraints about routing. However, privacy of the path is not the same as encryption of the payload. If your compliance or confidentiality requirements mandate end-to-end encryption, you should configure an IPsec VPN tunnel over the Direct Connect link. That overlay gives you the dedicated bandwidth and low latency of DX together with the cryptographic protection of VPN. An alternative sometimes discussed is using MACsec on physical links for Layer 2 protection, but MACsec is typically a link-layer feature and does not provide application-level end-to-end encryption across multiple hops. A common misconception is believing a private path removes the need for encryption. Always review regulatory controls: many standards require encryption of sensitive fields regardless of the path. Practically, you will plan key management, certificate rotation, and how encrypted tunnels interact with BGP and routing. Test both connectivity and the encryption overlay together to ensure route advertisement and traffic flow behave as expected with tunnels in place.

screens.title: Bringing a Direct Connect Link Online
screens.narratorSegment: Bringing a Direct Connect link online follows a clear sequence of operational steps. First, decide the Direct Connect location and the port speed you need based on bandwidth planning. Order the port or hosted connection and collect the provisioning details you will need: cross-connect ID, VLAN, and AWS-assigned port information. Second, coordinate with your colocation provider to establish the physical cross-connect between your router and the AWS router. Third, configure your on-prem router for BGP peering: set the ASN, BGP neighbor addresses, and any route filters you require. Fourth, create the appropriate virtual interfaces in the AWS console — private VIFs for VPC access, public VIFs for access to public AWS services. Fifth, test the session and validate route exchange, traffic flows, and failover behavior. Include a backup plan, such as an IPsec VPN or a second Direct Connect in another location, to ensure resilience. A frequent operational mistake is missing the VLAN number or cross-connect details in the order; keep a checklist to avoid provisioning delays. Finally, run a small-scale test migration or traffic burst to measure real performance and adjust routing preferences if necessary.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Estimate Savings and Time
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to estimate potential savings and performance improvements when comparing Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect for a 50 terabyte migration. Follow the steps: first, gather current per-gigabyte data transfer rates for both VPN and Direct Connect from your pricing resources. Second, compute the transfer time using the bits-over-bandwidth formula for a 100 megabit VPN and a 1 gigabit Direct Connect, applying 80 percent utilization to both. We walked through this math previously: 50 TB becomes 400 times ten to the twelfth bits. Dividing by 80 megabits per second yields roughly 5,000,000 seconds, or about 58 days for the 100 megabit VPN. For 1 gigabit at 80 percent, the result is about 5.8 days. Third, multiply the total data in gigabytes by the per-GB rate to get estimated transfer costs for each option. Fourth, compare time and cost to decide whether Direct Connect offers sufficient savings and schedule improvement to justify port and provisioning costs. A common pitfall is only comparing per-GB costs and ignoring time-to-completion; both factors influence the operational decision. After completing this activity, reflect on whether a staged transfer or additional temporary circuits could reduce migration time further.

Welcome. In this lesson we'll build an intuitive, practical understanding of AWS Direct Connect. Direct Connect is a physical, private network link into AWS that bypasses the public internet. That private path gives you consistent throughput, lower and more predictable latency, and often lower costs for moving large volumes of data. As you learn, think of Direct Connect as a private highway built between your data center and AWS. Unlike an encrypted tunnel over the internet, this highway keeps traffic off public routing, which reduces congestion, jitter, and packet loss for mission-critical services. We'll also cover when Direct Connect matters: hybrid applications that need LAN-like behavior, large data migrations and analytics transfers, low-latency use cases such as voice or trading systems, and situations where compliance forbids public internet transit. Finally, you'll see the basic elements that make a DX link work — the physical cross-connect at a Direct Connect location, Border Gateway Protocol peering, and logical virtual interfaces to reach VPCs or public AWS services. By the end, you'll be able to decide when Direct Connect is the right architectural choice and what components you must plan for. Consider: which of your current workloads would need the steadiness of a private highway versus the flexibility of a VPN?

In this section we'll set clear objectives so you know the skills you'll build. First, you'll be able to explain the core purpose and benefits of AWS Direct Connect: how a dedicated, private physical link changes performance, predictability, and cost profiles compared with internet-based VPN. You will learn to describe that Direct Connect bypasses the public internet, reducing congestion and making throughput and latency far more consistent for production services. Second, you will identify scenarios where Direct Connect matters most. These include hybrid cloud architectures that require near-LAN performance between on-premises systems and VPCs, large data migrations to S3 or analytics stores, and low-latency applications such as VoIP or trading platforms. You will also recognize compliance-driven use cases where data must not traverse public internet paths. Each objective ties theory to concrete operational decisions, so you'll practice mapping workloads to connectivity choices. Finally, we’ll introduce the verification milestone you can use to confirm competency: a short design exercise recommending Direct Connect or VPN for a specified workload. Keep thinking about a workload you manage and whether it needs the private highway Direct Connect provides.

This second objectives slide links each learning goal to practical actions you will perform. First, after explaining DX benefits you will compare measured metrics such as latency and throughput when evaluating connectivity options. For example, you will practice estimating transfer time for a large dataset and discuss how a predictable link reduces risk for migrations. Second, when identifying use cases, you'll learn to judge trade-offs: a VPN is flexible and quick to deploy but has variable performance; Direct Connect requires coordination and a physical connection but delivers consistent behavior. Third, differentiating the network principles means understanding that DX keeps traffic off public routing and uses BGP peering to exchange routes with AWS. You will set up an example BGP peering diagram to practice route choice and failover handling. Fourth, understanding components requires both physical and logical planning: ordering a cross-connect at a Direct Connect location, configuring the router, and creating virtual interfaces. The verification milestone asks you to draft a short design that justifies Direct Connect or VPN, and to list configuration items you would request from your colocation provider.

AWS Direct Connect is a service that provides a physical, private network connection between a customer's network and AWS. In plain language, picture a private highway between your data center and AWS that traffic uses instead of the public road network. This dedicates fiber capacity to your traffic and avoids the routing unpredictability of the public internet. The key claim to remember is this: Direct Connect gives you private, consistent connectivity — not automatic encryption. From an operational standpoint, that means you order a cross-connect at a Direct Connect location, install or request a port, then configure your edge router to peer with AWS using BGP. A common concrete example is database replication between on-premises systems and an Amazon VPC. With Direct Connect, the replication stream experiences fewer interruptions and steady throughput, so replication completes in predictable windows. A typical misconception is to assume Direct Connect encrypts traffic by default; it does not provide end-to-end encryption. If confidentiality is required, you should layer an IPsec VPN over the Direct Connect link. That combination gives you the privacy and low latency of a dedicated path with the encryption guarantees of a VPN. As you plan, ask: do I require encryption in transit? If yes, prepare to configure a VPN overlay or application-level encryption.

Comparing Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN helps you choose the right link for a workload. Site-to-Site VPN runs encrypted tunnels over the public internet. It is quick to deploy and can be a good short-term or backup option, but its performance depends on internet routing and can vary due to congestion and routing changes. Direct Connect, in contrast, establishes a private physical path that bypasses internet routing, delivering steady throughput and reduced latency. That steadiness matters for migrations, replication, and real-time applications. In cost terms, Direct Connect often reduces per-gigabyte transfer costs for high-volume traffic, but it does require port or circuit ordering and possibly colocation fees. A common operational pattern is to use Direct Connect as the primary link and keep VPN as a failover for resilience. Another misconception to avoid is assuming VPN always provides equal security to Direct Connect: VPN provides encryption over the internet, while Direct Connect provides a private path but not automatic encryption. For workloads requiring both privacy and encryption, the recommended approach is to run an IPsec VPN tunnel over the Direct Connect link. That design gives predictable performance and the encryption properties you need. When making a decision, weigh deployment time, monthly port costs, predictable SLAs, and the sensitivity of your data.

Hybrid cloud architectures combine on-premises resources with cloud-based services. Direct Connect helps these environments behave like a unified network by offering consistent, low-jitter connectivity between your data center and AWS. This matters when applications require frequent synchronous calls, for example between a local identity service and a cloud-hosted application, or when you run distributed databases that replicate between sites. With a Direct Connect link and BGP peering, your on-prem routes and VPC routes can be exchanged so that application traffic follows a predictable path. Large-scale data transfers are one of the clearest use cases for Direct Connect. Moving many terabytes or petabytes over the public internet can be slow, unpredictable, and expensive. A typical planning step is to assume 70–80 percent utilization to capture realistic throughput. A common error is to assume line rate equals effective throughput. Always apply utilization and overhead for protocol and storage performance when estimating. Finally, consider parallelization or staging transfers: using multiple connections or dedicated appliances for bulk import can shorten windows and distribute load safely.
